item.title: The Journey of Over Scoping
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
My First Game Jam#

First things first, our game is playable on itch for anyone who wishes to give it a go.

As I have begun my game development journey, I have immersed myself within the culture and the media surrounding games and making games. Not like I wasn't wholeheartedly subscribed to video games as a hobby to begin with, as I sure have played my fair share. Moreover, I have begun to peek behind the curtain. Found out what drives the game culture from behind the scenes. One such thing I have recently discovered is game jams. I have heard of hackathons and the like from university where all the plucky comp-sci students would amble around like MonsterTM-infused zombies trying to finish... something. Never quite got the appeal. Then by happenstance I found out that Bevy does game jams for every even version release. Last year I played some of the games for Bevy's 0.18 release jam. Now, boy howdy, was I impressed! These games came out in the span of 9 days and most of them were in a playable and enjoyable state.

This was in the beginning days of my foray into game development. I had just really decided to tap into my atrocious creative side and start thinking outside the box of what shall I watch tonight. I may have said before that I have always fantasized about creating things. Many, many, oh so many abandoned projects to my name. Physical projects that never got beyond a wistful ideation in the shower, creative works that never saw the light of day. Hidden in my imagination, mostly because I can't render anything to save my life. Now, spending most of my working day on a computer, one would think that I wanted to find a different outlet. But they would be wrong, see, as game development is an interesting mix of technical, artistic, and creative problem-solving that just really gets my engine going. Sure it is mostly behind a keyboard but the skills learned transfer to oh so many other things. Music, art, and creativity abound and are useful in oh so many ways.

Though I digress. Since playing those games from Bevy Jam 7, when I first discovered Bevy (at a convenient time, no less, as I had only just started wanting to get into games), I figured a game jam might be interesting. The announcement came almost unexpectedly, though. By happenstance I checked on the Bevy Discord while walking the dogs and found out the jam had been announced a few days earlier! See, I had forgotten about the jam held every even version deal. Now I have only been dedicatedly making games for upwards of a year and am by no means good. So unlike the savants that frequent the Bevy Discord, I needed a team. I am a systems engineer by trade, and thus work with a bunch of other quite quirky and nerdy folks who, if I asked, would work on a game jam at a moment's notice. Life is better with friends after all, and luckily for me they had plenty of time for this 9-day walk through purgatory (subtle foreshadowing). Or they had none at all, but still did it anyways cause friends are cool and they all deserve a big golden star for everything they do. So all this to say, I found a team in a matter of days, a handful of individuals ready to make a game.

Our team was interesting: a comp-sci graduate who had won a game jam in high school, but never programmed in Rust before. A physics graduate who has a baby on the way any moment yet really wanted to do art when I asked them super last minute to join. A fellow chemical engineer who has never really coded in their life but makes dope ass sounds and music. And another engineer, who has dabbled in game making before but never in Rust and had to find the time in between writing for NaNoWriMo (which I found out this month involves people trying to write whole ass books in a month). So with our last-minute team put together, we eagerly awaited the theme announcement. The Discord was all aflutter with what the theme could be, as voting was visible and transparent to the whole community. I had my bets on synthetic environment (had some good ideas for it too), until again, on a walk with the dogs, I found out it was Alchemy. Now there are endless possibilities of games that one could make with alchemy as a theme. Anything from witchy wonders of grim delight, to futuristic synthesoids running amok in New York City creating dastardly mixtures of potent poisons. And this is where our biggest hurdle would present itself.

But what shall we make?#

My partner, as I was chatting with them about the upcoming jam, suggested we do an Overcooked-style game, but with potions and potentially angry customers. I was immediately hooked on the idea. So two days after the theme announcement, our team met and started discussing scope. As that is what every good dev team does when they wanna make a game, right? Talk about what the hell we're supposed to make and what it should look like. I pitched my partner's Overcooked idea, and everyone seemed hooked as well. So over an hour or so, we discussed the ins and outs of what this had to look like. We talked art, we talked mechanics, we talked about the meaning of life and 42 other things for what this game should be and ultimately came up with this.

Name TBD Scope#

Run an alchemy potion shop and craft potions for your customers. You are playing as a young witch/wizard who is looking after the shop for your old wizened grandpa while they are at wizardcon. Customers will enter the shop and pseudo-randomly give an order for a potion to be brewed.

Art Style:

  • Meme art style 2010s (Thick lines, sparse detail, cute and unhinged)
  • Top-down 2D view
  • Map with multiple layers in Z direction

Game Mechanics TODO:

  • [] Each customer presents a desired potion using iconography
  • [] Each potion is made in a cauldron
  • [] Each potion is made up of up to 4 ingredients
  • [] Each potion will require one main base ingredient
  • [] Conflicting effects in a cauldron will explode the cauldron
  • [] Overbrewing a potion catches the cauldron on fire
  • [] burnt down and exploded cauldrons must be repaired
  • [] Any extra ingredients will be modifiers that alter primary ingredients' effects
  • [] A recipe book will show primary effects and secondary effects of each item
  • [] An herb garden to grow herbs used in potions
  • [] A day-night cycle, players need to brew potions for customers at night
  • [] Grow herbs during the day and take a nap to end the day and start the next night
  • [] Herbs will be ready for harvest the next night
  • [] The player needs to not burn down the shop for 8 moons to win
  • [] Players can exchange herbs by using cat workers to go out and find new ingredients for ones they already have

Now this doesn't seem so bad, right? Yeah, we thought so. We thought we were all hot shit for sure. This game is small! There are only like 15 rules to make the mechanics, and those can be boiled down to like a handful of similar systems that feed off each other. This is where that foreshadowing comes to mind. This game is indeed not small. Between the mechanics and the artists discovering how hard it is to make art in 9 days while also never having made a sprite sheet before, the scope is relatively massive. This smol scope further evolved when the artists made a little list of what they all had to do.

Art TODO:

  • [] Ingredient Book & Book UI
  • [] Ingredient Sprites
  • [] Customer Demand Sprites
  • [] Customers
  • [] Potion Shop
  • [] Cauldron
  • [] Drying Racks
  • [] Mortar & Pestle
  • [] Flasks
  • [] Grow Beds
  • [] Plant Sprites

The artists tried their best, and honestly, it was well put together. The art fit the theme of the game masterfully. Were the sprite sheets hard to navigate programmatically? Oh yes, yes they were. But lessons learned: sprite sheets need a standard established from the outset. Artists and programmers need a crisp, clean line of communication on what the program needs, and what the artists can render out. Now I wouldn't say I neglected to talk to the art team and discuss what the art should be and what a sprite sheet should look like. But I was indeed very wishy-washy on what the sprite sheet layout should be. Which ultimately led us to this: the art was gorgeous. Making it work in game was a nightmare.

Am I right though? The art is stellar. The pictures are exactly what we were looking for. But then we ran into issues on making the sprite sheet itself. One artist did the sheet up above. But then another did this wondrous artwork below. We wanted to use this as a border around the shop that the player runs. Alas, since one artist exported the sprite sheet and we pulled it into our map editor as an image, we couldn't fit in the border art into the map as we hastily tried to submit the game last minute. But it deserves to be seen, so here it is!

But then the other programmer and I needed to make it work in game. And this then led to just a bunch of pixel hunting. Each sprite is of a different size, as one can see. Nothing is really square, and the sprite sheet is a mix of animation columns and rows and static assets. So, to make all this work we had to build a sprite sheet utility to work with it all!

Our methodology was to just hard-code in where in the sprite sheet an asset was, and work from there specifying the columns and rows for each type of animation. The Bevy Flock group has a really well-done 2D template that goes into detail on how to set up sprite animation like this. We based our game off of this template. Though I think at the time we started the jam it wasn't updated to Bevy 0.20.

So what we ended up doing was constructing sprites as a scene when entering the gameplay state of the game: the state where the witch Celeste is in the shop and can move around. The player character, Celeste, uses the same idea, as would the customers if we ever got around to putting them in the game.

/// This little function here is the `Base` scene. It is used to define what
/// a `Station` is and what it should look like.
pub fn stations(kind: StationKind, assets: &StationAssets) -> impl Scene {
    let sheet = assets.sheet(kind);
    let layout = assets.layout(kind);
    let transform = Transform::from_scale(Vec3::splat(kind.spec().scale));

    bsn! {
        @stations_base_scene(kind)
        Sprite {
            image: sheet,
            texture_atlas: {
                Some(TextureAtlasTemplate {
                    layout: layout.into(),
                    index: 0
                })
            }
        }
        transform
    }
}

/// This is the resource that we used to pull assets from
/// the sprite sheets.
#[derive(Resource, Asset, Clone, Reflect)]
#[reflect(Resource)]
pub struct StationAssets {
    /// One handle per station kind, in `StationKind::ALL` order. Currently all
    /// kinds share the same source sheet but use different atlas regions.
    #[dependency]
    sheets: Vec<Handle<Image>>,
    /// One atlas layout per kind, in the same order. Built in code
    /// with `Assets::add`, not loaded so no #[dependency]
    layouts: Vec<Handle<TextureAtlasLayout>>,
    /// For debug and primitives construction
    pub debug_mesh: Vec<Handle<Mesh>>,
    pub debug_material: Vec<Handle<ColorMaterial>>,
}

/// This implementation is used for constructors that will
/// pull information for constructing the sprite in game.
impl StationAssets {
    pub fn sheet(&self, kind: StationKind) -> Handle<Image> {
        self.sheets[kind.index()].clone()
    }

    pub fn layout(&self, kind: StationKind) -> Handle<TextureAtlasLayout> {
        self.layouts[kind.index()].clone()
    }

    pub fn mesh(&self, kind: StationKind) -> Handle<Mesh> {
        self.debug_mesh[kind.index()].clone()
    }

    pub fn material(&self, kind: StationKind) -> Handle<ColorMaterial> {
        self.debug_material[kind.index()].clone()
    }
}

/// Finally, our FromWorld is used to pull the spritesheets from
/// the game world. Then store them as a `StationAssets` for use later.
impl FromWorld for StationAssets {
    fn from_world(world: &mut World) -> Self {
        // The lists below are looked up by `kind as usize`, so `ALL` must match
        // the enum's order. This catches a mismatch in dev builds.
        for (i, kind) in StationKind::ALL.iter().enumerate() {
            debug_assert_eq!(
                kind.index(),
                i,
                "StationKind::ALL must list variants in declaration order."
            );
        }

        // A texture atlas is a fancy way to split a single image into a grid of related images.
        // an example is found here: https://github.com/bevyengine/bevy/blob/latest/examples/2d/texture_atlas.rs
        let layouts = {
            let mut layouts = world.resource_mut::<Assets<TextureAtlasLayout>>();
            StationKind::ALL
                .iter()
                .map(|kind| {
                    let sheet = kind.sprite_sheet();
                    layouts.add(TextureAtlasLayout::from_grid(
                        sheet.frame_size,
                        sheet.columns,
                        sheet.rows,
                        Some(UVec2::splat(sheet.padding)),
                        Some(sheet.offset),
                    ))
                })
                .collect()
        };

        let debug_mesh = {
            let mut meshes = world.resource_mut::<Assets<Mesh>>();
            StationKind::ALL
                .iter()
                .map(|kind| meshes.add(Circle::new(kind.spec().size.x as f32)))
                .collect()
        };

        let debug_material = {
            let mut materials = world.resource_mut::<Assets<ColorMaterial>>();
            StationKind::ALL
                .iter()
                .map(|kind| {
                    materials.add(ColorMaterial {
                        color: kind.spec().color,
                        alpha_mode: AlphaMode2d::Blend,
                        ..default()
                    })
                })
                .collect()
        };

        let assets = world.resource::<AssetServer>();

        let sheet = assets
            .load_builder()
            .with_settings(|settings: &mut ImageLoaderSettings| {
                settings.sampler = ImageSampler::nearest();
            })
            .load("images/SpriteSheet.png");

        let sheets: Vec<Handle<Image>> = StationKind::ALL.iter().map(|_| sheet.clone()).collect();

        Self {
            sheets,
            layouts,
            debug_mesh,
            debug_material,
        }
    }
}

/// Our TextureAtlases were quite non-uniform. So, to get
/// around that we synced our assets with the size of the
/// image used for the sprite sheet.
fn sync_atlas_size(
    station_assets: Option<Res<StationAssets>>,
    images: Res<Assets<Image>>,
    mut layouts: ResMut<Assets<TextureAtlasLayout>>,
) {
    let Some(station_assets) = station_assets else {
        return;
    };

    for kind in StationKind::ALL {
        let Some(image) = images.get(&station_assets.sheets[kind.index()]) else {
            continue;
        };

        let Some(mut layout) = layouts.get_mut(&station_assets.layouts[kind.index()]) else {
            continue;
        };

        // read the png dimensions
        let image_size = image.size();
        if layout.size != image_size {
            layout.size = image_size;
        }
    }
}

So those functions up above are just helpers that pull in the sprite sheet asset from the game world and then do some magic in reading pixels and sheet layout to return an animation. Ideally, we would have had separate animation states that pulled from elsewhere in the sheet as well, but again, time and scope are dastardly enemies.

As you can see, we also have some cute little customer designs. The other programmer and I ended up spending so much time trying to sort out spawning characters and making the game interactable that we didn't end up making anything to interact with. However, the other programmer Justin did come in with a last-minute save to make the plant bed interactable. So we ended up with a cute little witch and her cat who you can make walk around the shop and pick up plants.

So, what did we learn?#

Well, I learned how to have a good time under stress. Staying up till 2 am trying to fix merge conflicts cause I forgot how to work git that late. Chatting with the programmers and the artists I worked with and laughing at the ram shamble that we put together. Nine days may seem like a lot, but it really is no time at all.

One thing I found really helpful throughout was teaching Rust as well as learning it myself. The other programmer that I worked with for this jam is a code genius. Able to read and understand lines of code like it is the air that they breathe. But they had never worked in Rust before, and I have even though I have a lot left to learn. So, to be able to teach a new language to this gifted individual gave me a new frame of reference for understanding code.

I like the expression that the best way to understand something is to try and teach it. So being able to talk code with a technical savant who understands, but doesn't quite know the intricacies of Rust, is a great way to learn by teaching I think. When I talked with the artists after the jam, they mentioned how much they learned as well by sitting down and making time to use the tools that they had been meaning to practise. The jam was the perfect excuse to make time for learning and development. Looking back at the rules, too, it seems our little team took this jam to heart and embodied learning, even if we didn't finish our little game.

item.title: Game Two of Twenty
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
EDIT: Updated to reflect the change in godot-rust to a pure bevy build of the game.

Alright, here we go#

Game two, check it out on the projects page. This one was a bit much on my end, and it's still not done. Filled with a few bugs, and showing some wear and tear in terms of how it plays. But overall I think I need to move on. This game took long, much longer than pong and I need to learn to be comfortable with letting things go. So for all it's worth this is it. Fly Away! a game where a crow has to fly away from their natural enemies, tree branches and great horned owls.

This game was a mit more intensive than my last. Using actual assets and sounds and models, very professional very artistic. And since I am no artist, yet, I sourced a great deal of these assets from the wonderful world of itch. This one was a bit of an experement to say the least. I started in godot-rust, make a working game that has a serious lack of polish, but then though (with the release of bevy 0.20) why not just make it in bevy. I know that godot is production ready, able to ship some amazing games already and there is a lot of skill and talent behind godot. But, I want to make something fun, and I want to force myself to actually learn to code along with all the artistic endavours I am trying out. Just wait for the pixel art travesties I will subject you all to the next game.

Now I used mostly open licence no attribution assets, but attribution should be given for these wonderful products. Such all the assets I used came from the following creators.

  • Background from Meowtastic
  • Music from FarBeyond Studio
  • Sfx from my partner
  • Sprites from SkaldingDelight for the branches, SeethingSwarm for the crow, PeakPixels for the owls.

For this game, I drew a large amount of my inspiration and guidance from marcs-sus and their implementation of the game. I do like the wizards flying around shooting particles everywhere. Now, I am no where near a state to make particle effects or fancy graphics implementations. Just getting the game to save the high score was hard enough. Working with the serde crate though I eventually bumbled my way through it. Still have much to learn though, at some point I may be good enough to make something akin to the nemisis system, or the alien isolation system, or some sort of save scumming mechanism to make future games more interesting. But that is just me waxing all poetic about a future I don't even know about or care to think of right now.

All in all, I am learning that there is so much that goes into every little aspect of making a game. From the art, to the feel, and to the essence of what the game is it all really matters. So, am I ready for the GMTK jam in 2027? No, not even close. But for now, have fun making a crow fly up and down. This game took me better part of three weeks after the first pong game. Now is that timeline to long for a jetpack joyride clone? Probably, but this is only really my second game I made start to finish. So as I prepare for the crunch that is GMTK next year, lets see if I can cut those production times down.
